Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

derivations.claim: By openness choose $R>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,2R)\subset U$. Continuity of $X$ and $DX$ at $q_0$ gives finite $M,L\ge0$ bounding $\|X\|$ on $\overline B(q_0,R)$ and $\|DX\|$ on $B(q_0,2R)$. By [F1] $X$ is totally differentiable there, and [F2] applied to the convex ball $B(q_0,2R)$ gives $\|X(u)-X(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for $u,v\in\overline B(q_0,R)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ with $M\delta\le R/2$ and $L\delta<1$, and let $\mathcal C:=\{\gamma\in C([-\delta,\delta],\mathbb R^m):\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)\text{ for every }t\}$ with the supremum norm. It is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(\gamma_k)$, [F5] gives the pointwise limit $\gamma(t)\in\mathbb R^m$; the supremum-Cauchy estimate, passed to that pointwise limit, gives uniform convergence to $\gamma$. The limit is continuous: given $\varepsilon>0$ and $t_0$, choose $k$ with $\|\gamma_k-\gamma\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then continuity gives $\rho>0$ such that $\|\gamma_k(t)-\gamma_k(t_0)\|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\rho$; the triangle inequality yields $\|\gamma(t)-\gamma(t_0)\|<\varepsilon$. Also $\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)$ for every $t$, since this Euclidean ball is closed and each $\gamma_k(t)$ lies in it. Thus $\gamma\in\mathcal C$. For $p\in\overline B(q_0,R/2)$ define $T_p\gamma(t):=p+\int_0^t X(\gamma(s))\,ds$. The integrand is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. Then $T_p$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, since $\|T_p\gamma(t)-q_0\|\le\|p-q_0\|+M|t|\le R$, and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$.

Starting at the constant curve $\gamma_0(t)=p$, iterate $\gamma_{k+1}=T_p\gamma_k$. If $\kappa=L\delta<1$, then $\|\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_k\|_\infty\le\kappa^k\|\gamma_1-\gamma_0\|_\infty$; the geometric tail bound makes $(\gamma_k)$ uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $\phi(\cdot,p)\in\mathcal C$ is a fixed point by the contraction bound. Any two fixed points have distance at most $\kappa$ times that distance, so they coincide.

For $g(s)=X(\phi(s,p))$, continuity and [F3] make every component Riemann integrable. At an interior $t$, the difference quotient of $\phi(t,p)=p+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ differs from $g(t)$ by at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|$, which tends to zero by continuity; thus $\partial_t\phi=X(\phi)$. Conversely any $C^1$ solution staying in the ball satisfies the fixed-point equation by [F4], so uniqueness of the fixed point is uniqueness of the IVP.

If $p,p'$ lie in $\overline B(q_0,R/2)$, subtract their fixed-point equations from step 3.1 and take suprema to obtain $\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty\le\|p-p'\|+L\delta\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, division gives the local Lipschitz estimate $(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|p-p'\|$.

Whenever the compositions remain in the chosen ball, both $t\mapsto\phi(t+s,p)$ and $t\mapsto\phi(t,\phi(s,p))$ solve the same IVP at $t=0$, with initial value $\phi(s,p)$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 gives the local flow law; setting $t=-s$ gives the local inverse relation.

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

derivations.claim: For $m=0$, define $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton consisting of the empty coordinate tuple, denoted $0$, with its unique vector-space structure and norm $\|0\|=0$. Its open subsets are empty or the singleton; the empty domain has no initial point and all assertions there are vacuous. On the singleton both fields necessarily equal zero. Define $\phi_X^t(0)=\phi_Y^t(0)=0$ for every real $t$. These are the unique solution curves and satisfy the flow law. Every map into this zero vector space has the unique zero linear map as total derivative, since its differentiability remainder is identically zero; iterating gives continuous derivatives through order two. Thus the flows are jointly $C^2$, $J$ is the unique endomorphism of $\mathbb R^0$, which is also its identity $I_0$, and $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X)J=0$. The bracket and both transport expressions are zero, and both flow compositions are the identity. This proves every assertion for $m=0$ without invoking the positive-dimensional suppliers. In the remaining steps assume $m\ge1$.

For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. The integral equations from [F1] and the one-variable fundamental theorem applied to $\theta\mapsto X(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))$ give $$\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_0^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds,\quad A_h(s):=\int_0^1DX(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))\,d\theta.$$ The segments lie in $K$ after shrinking the initial ball and time interval. The local Lipschitz estimate in [F1] gives $\sup_t\|\Delta_h(t)\|=O(\|h\|)$. Uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$ from [F4] makes $A_h(s)$ converge uniformly to $DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ as $h\to0$.

Let $\mathcal I=[-\delta,\delta]$ and let $\mathcal C_1=C(\mathcal I,M_m(\mathbb R))$ with the supremum operator norm. This space is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(J_k)$, each matrix entry at each $s$ is Cauchy because $|A_{ij}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; [F5] applied to the $m^2$ entries gives a pointwise matrix limit $J(s)$, and the uniform Cauchy estimate passed to each entry gives uniform convergence of all entries. Each limit entry is continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ argument for uniform limits of continuous functions. The finite-coordinate bound $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ then gives uniform operator-norm convergence, so $J\in\mathcal C_1$. The space is nonempty because it contains the constant zero matrix curve. Put $A_0(s):=DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ and define $T(J)(t):=I_m+\int_0^t A_0(s)J(s)\,ds$. It maps $\mathcal C_1$ into itself and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta<1$. By [F6], it has a unique fixed point $J$. Define $R_h(t):=\Delta_h(t)-J(t)h$. Subtracting the integral equations and writing the integrand difference as $(A_h-A_0)\Delta_h+A_0R_h$ gives $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+\delta\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\|\Delta_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|)$, by step 1.2 and uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$. Thus $D_q\phi_X^t(p)=J(t,p)$. The continuous integrand in the equation for $J$ has average over $[t,t+h]$ tending to its value at $t$: the quotient error is at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|DX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s,p)-DX(\phi_X^t(p))J(t,p)\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(p))J$ and $J(0,p)=I_m$.

Write $J_h(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $J_0(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p)$. Subtracting their integral equations gives $J_h-J_0=\int_0^t A_0(J_h-J_0)\,ds+\int_0^t(A_h-A_0)J_h\,ds$, where $A_h=DX(\phi_h)$, $A_0=DX(\phi_0)$, $\phi_h=\phi_X^s(p+h)$, and $\phi_0=\phi_X^s(p)$. The line-segment chain rule and Newton–Leibniz supplier claims in [F2]–[F3], applied entrywise to $DX$ along the segment from $\phi_0$ to $\phi_h$, give the exact formula $A_h-A_0=\int_0^1D^2X(\phi_0+\theta(\phi_h-\phi_0))[\phi_h-\phi_0,\cdot]\,d\theta$ and therefore $\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\le M_2\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty$. By [F1], $\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty=O(\|h\|)$; the integral equation gives $\|J_h\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}$. Absorbing the first integral using $L\delta<1$ yields $J_h-J_0=O(\|h\|)$ uniformly in time. Uniform continuity of $D^2X$ on $K$, the same line-segment formula, and $\phi_h-\phi_0=J_0h+o(\|h\|)$ from step 2.1 now give $A_h-A_0=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|)$ uniformly, and hence $(A_h-A_0)J_h=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,J_0(\cdot)]+o(\|h\|)$. For each base point $p$, define $\mathcal C_2=C(\mathcal I,\operatorname{Bil}(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^m))$ with the supremum bilinear-operator norm. The coordinatewise completeness proof of step 2.1 applies with $m^3$ coefficients, so $\mathcal C_2$ is complete; it is nonempty because it contains the zero bilinear-map curve. The map $(\mathcal T K)(t)[u,v]:=\int_0^t\big(A_0(s)K(s)[u,v]+D^2X(\phi_0(s))[J_0(s)u,J_0(s)v]\big)\,ds$ is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$ on $\mathcal C_2$. By [F6] it has a unique fixed point $K_p$. Subtracting its equation evaluated at $(h,v)$ from the equation for $J_h-J_0$ gives $R_h:=J_h-J_0-K_p[h,\cdot]$ with $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+o(\|h\|)$, so $R_h=o(\|h\|)$. Therefore $D_pJ[h](v)=K_p[h,v]$, and $K_p$ is the second derivative $D_q^2\phi_X$. Its equation makes it bilinear. The coefficients, forcing, $\phi_p$, and $J_p$ vary continuously in $p$ uniformly for $s\in\mathcal I$; for fixed-point maps $T_p$ with contraction constant $L\delta$, $\|K_p-K_{p'}\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|T_p(K_{p'})-T_{p'}(K_{p'})\|_\infty\to0$. The integral equation gives continuity in $t$ as well. Thus the second derivatives in $q$ are continuous.

Let $V(t):=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and $W(t):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)$. By [F2] and the variational equation, $V'=DY(\phi_X^t)X(\phi_X^t)$ and $W'=DX(\phi_X^t)W$. The identity $[X,Y]=0$ makes $V$ solve this same linear equation with $V(0)=W(0)=Y(q)$; uniqueness from the contraction argument gives $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$.

On the open interior of the chosen time and initial-point neighborhood, step 2.1 gives $D_q\phi_X=J$ and $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X)J$, while step 3.1 gives the continuous second derivative $D_qJ=K$. The chain rule [F2] applied to $\partial_t\phi_X=X(\phi_X)$ gives $\partial_{q_i}\partial_t\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)Je_i$, and the variational equation gives $\partial_t\partial_{q_i}\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)Je_i$; also $\partial_t^2\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)X(\phi_X)$. Hence all first- and second-order coordinate partial derivatives of $\phi_X$ exist and are continuous there. Apply [F7] pointwise first to $\phi_X$ and then to its first-derivative map: its Jacobian is the matrix of first partials, and the Jacobian of that map is the continuous array of second partials. Thus $\phi_X$ is jointly $C^2$.

For fixed $t$, the curve $s\mapsto\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ has derivative $D\phi_X^t\,Y(\phi_Y^s(q))=Y(\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q)))$ by step 3.2, and starts at $\phi_X^t(q)$. It is therefore the $Y$-flow from that initial point; IVP uniqueness from [F1] yields $\phi_X^t\phi_Y^s(q)=\phi_Y^s\phi_X^t(q)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. For $k\in\{1,2\}$, a $C^k$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is $k$ times continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For a $C^1$ scalar function $S:W\to\mathbb R$ on an open $W\subseteq U$, its differential is the one-form defined by

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then $E$ is connected ([[def-connected-r]]) if and
only if $E$ is **order-convex** ([[def-interval]]), that is, if and only if

$$x, z \in E \text{ and } x \le w \le z \;\Longrightarrow\; w \in E .$$

**On the word "interval".** Order-convexity is exactly the defining property
that [[def-interval]] proves for each of its nine forms, and in that sense the
theorem says that the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals. The
converse classification, that every order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is empty
or one of the nine forms, is true and is explicitly **not proved anywhere in
this library**; [[def-interval]] records that omission in its own remarks. So
the statement proved below is the equivalence with order-convexity, and the
phrase "is an interval" is to be read as "is order-convex" throughout this page.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

derivations.claim: Use the local first integrals in the Statement. Write $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\omega_j dx_j$ in the fixed Euclidean coordinates and set $w=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{n+1})$ and $Z_j=e_j-(\omega_j/|w|^2)w$. These globally defined $C^2$ vector fields are horizontal and span $\ker\omega$ at each point, since their matrix is the orthogonal projection onto that kernel. On every neighborhood supplied by the hypothesis, $dS=\mu\omega$ has nonzero derivative, and each $Z_j$-flow preserves $S$ as long as its trajectory remains there, by [F3]. Its derivative therefore preserves horizontal tangent vectors there: differentiating $S(\phi_j^t(x))=S(x)$ gives $dS_{\phi_j^t(x)}D\phi_j^t(x)v=dS_xv=0$ for horizontal $v$. The compact image of any finite flow trajectory has a finite subcover by such neighborhoods; a sufficiently fine finite subdivision of its compact time interval puts each subtrajectory in one of them. This follows directly from compactness: otherwise shrinking subintervals failing the subdivision would have a limiting time whose neighborhood contains them. Composing the local derivative identities obtains preservation over the full duration. Local flow uniqueness makes these continuations consistent, and [F2] gives $C^2$ dependence on durations and initial points wherever the finite composition is defined.

Fix $q\in U$ and a neighborhood $W$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ as in the hypothesis. Since $dS_q=\mu(q)\omega_q\ne0$, apply [L1] to $x\mapsto S(x)-S(q)$ with ambient dimension $n+1$ and target dimension $1$; after choosing the solved coordinate, its zero set is a local $C^1$ graph plaque $P$ through $q$, parameterized by its $n$ free coordinates. Let $\pi$ be projection to those free coordinates. Choose $n$ of the fields $Z_j$ that form a basis of $\ker\omega_q=\ker dS_q$, and for $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ near $0$ let $E(s)$ be the endpoint at $q$ of the successive local flows of these fields for durations $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. Shrink the open duration domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ so all flow segments stay in $W$. Step 1.1 shows that each flow preserves $S$, so $E(D)\subseteq P$; moreover $DE(0)$ has the chosen basis as its columns. The differential $D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is therefore an invertible $n\times n$ matrix, because $D\pi_q$ is an isomorphism from the tangent space of the graph plaque to its free-coordinate space. Choose an open neighborhood $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $y_0=\pi(q)$ and shrink $D$ so that the target-augmented map $H:D\times Y\to\mathbb R^n$, $H(s,y):=\pi(E(s))-y$, is defined. It satisfies $H(0,y_0)=0$ and its solved block $D_sH(0,y_0)=D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2n$ and target dimension $n<2n$, permuting inputs to $(y,s)$ so $y$ is free and $s$ is solved. For every $y$ near $y_0$ this gives $s(y)$ with $\pi(E(s(y)))=y$; uniqueness of the graph plaque then says the endpoints $E(s(y))$ fill a relative neighborhood of $q$ in $P$. Each is reachable by a finite word of horizontal flows inside $W$. Conversely, a horizontal path preserves the local $S$ on each short subarc in a first-integral neighborhood by [F3]. Thus near each parameter value its image lies in the relative plaque neighborhood just shown to be reachable by such a finite word. The finite-word orbits are equivalence classes by flow reversal and concatenation, so their preimages along the path are relatively open in its interval domain. By [F4], connectedness of that interval forces one class. Hence every point horizontally reachable from $q$ lies in its finite-word orbit; the reverse inclusion follows because every word is a horizontal concatenation.

For a fixed finite word $\alpha$ of length $m\ge1$, write $F_\alpha:O_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to U$ for its endpoint map from $q$, on the open set of admissible duration tuples. Each duration derivative is a field vector transported by the later flows and is horizontal by step 1.1. Near any $s\in O_\alpha$, continuity puts the endpoint image in a neighborhood with the first integral $S$ from the hypothesis; hence $D(S\circ F_\alpha)=0$. On a small convex parameter ball, [F3] makes $S\circ F_\alpha$ constant. Coordinatewise density in [F5] supplies a closed box with rational endpoints containing $s$ in its interior and contained in that ball. Its image under $F_\alpha$ is compact by [F6], lies in one level of $S$, and has empty interior in $U$: a nonempty open subset of that image would make $S$ constant on an open set, contradicting $dS=\mu\omega\ne0$. Thus the image is a closed nowhere-dense subset of $U$. Enumerate the finite-word/rational-box pairs by the finite-level coding in [F5]; for an admissible box whose compact image has empty interior record that image, and otherwise record the empty set. Include the singleton $\{q\}$ for the empty word. This sequence $(K_j)$ of closed nowhere-dense sets covers $\mathcal O(q)$, since every duration tuple admits the small box just constructed. No countable atlas or choice of first integrals is needed for the enumeration.

Let $V$ be any nonempty open subset of $U$. By [F5], choose an initial rational open ball $B_{-1}$ with $\overline{B_{-1}}\subset V$. Recursively, for each $j\ge0$, choose the first rational ball $B_j=B(c_j,r_j)$ in the fixed enumeration such that $\overline{B_j}\subset B_{j-1}\setminus K_j$ and $0<r_j<2^{-j}$. Such a ball exists: $K_j$ is closed with empty interior, so $B_{j-1}\setminus K_j$ is a nonempty open set, which contains a rational ball with closed ball inside it and arbitrarily small radius by [F5]. For $k>j$, the later centers lie in $B_j$, so $|c_k-c_j|<r_j<2^{-j}$; hence $(c_j)$ is Cauchy. By [F7] it has a limit $p$, and each tail of the sequence lies in the closed ball $\overline{B_j}$, so $p\in\overline{B_j}$ for every $j$. These closed balls lie in $V$ and satisfy $\overline{B_j}\cap K_j=\varnothing$, so $p\in V\setminus\bigcup_jK_j$. Each selection is the least natural-number index satisfying explicit conditions, so it uses no choice axiom. Since the $K_j$ cover $\mathcal O(q)$, step 2.1 shows $p$ is not horizontally reachable from $q$ even by a path in $U$, and therefore not by one in $V$. This proves the asserted conclusion for every nonempty open $V$, using no global first integral or choice axiom.
